title: Poincare isogeny decomposition and simple factors
statement: Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field]. A positive-dimensional abelian variety $C/k$ [def-sc-abelian-variety] is called $k$-simple if it has no abelian subvariety over $k$ of dimension strictly between $0$ and $\dim C$; an abelian subvariety means a closed $k$-subgroup scheme which is itself an abelian variety [def-sc-group-scheme]. Every abelian variety $A/k$ admits a finite family of $k$-simple abelian varieties $C_1,\ldots,C_r$ and a $k$-isogeny $u:\prod_{i=1}^r C_i\to A$ [def-sc-isogeny]; the product is the zero abelian variety when $r=0$. Every nonzero $k$-group-scheme homomorphism between two $k$-simple abelian varieties is an isogeny. Every $k$-isogeny $f:X\to Y$ of abelian varieties has a $k$-isogeny $g:Y\to X$ and an integer $n>0$ with $g\circ f=[n]_X$ and $f\circ g=[n]_Y$, where $[n]$ denotes multiplication by $n$ [def-sc-mult-n].

source.place: Chapter I, Proposition 10.1 and the simple-factor discussion following Remark 10.2, printed pp.42–43; Remark 8.6, printed p.36 (quasi-inverse isogenies).

proof.text: We first construct a complement to a nonzero proper abelian subvariety $i:B\hookrightarrow A$. By [lem-sfb-abelian-inclusion-multiple-retraction], choose $n>0$ and $r:A\to B$ with $ri=[n]_B$. Abelian varieties are commutative by [lem-sc-av-commutative], so $q=[n]_A-ir$ is a homomorphism. The group laws [def-sc-group-scheme, def-sc-mult-n] give $qi=0$ and $rq=[n]_Br-ri r=0$. Let $j:C\hookrightarrow A$ be the scheme-theoretic image of $q$, an abelian variety by [lem-sfb-abelian-hom-image-dimension]. Since $rq=0$, $rj=0$: the defining ideal of $\ker r$ pulls back to zero under $q$, so it lies in the kernel of $\mathcal O_A\to q_*\mathcal O_A$, the ideal defining $C$.

source.place: Proposition 8.23 and Theorem 8.24, pp.152–153; image construction replacing the potentially nonsmooth kernel complement by Im([n]-ir).

proof.text: The addition homomorphism $s:B\times_kC\to A$, $(b,c)\mapsto i(b)+j(c)$, has abelian-variety source by [lem-sfb-abelian-finite-product]. It is surjective: $[n]_A=ir+q$ factors through $s$, and $[n]_A$ is surjective by [lem-sc-mult-n-isogeny]. Its kernel is isomorphic to $B\times_A C$ by $(b,c)\mapsto(b,-c)$, with the inverse given by the same formula. As $rj=0$, this intersection is a closed subscheme of $B[n]$: on it $[n]_Bb=ri(b)=rj(c)=0$. Thus it is finite, since $B[n]$ is finite by the same cited theorem; a closed subscheme of the spectrum of a finite-dimensional algebra has a quotient coordinate algebra of finite dimension. Consequently $s$ is an isogeny [def-sc-isogeny].

source.place: I Proposition 10.1, printed p.42, simple-factor discussion p.43, and Remark 8.6, p.36; scheme-theoretic details as specified in each step.

proof.text: For use in induction, $\dim A=\dim B+\dim C$: apply the kernel dimension formula [lem-sfb-abelian-hom-image-dimension] to the surjective map $s$, whose finite kernel has dimension zero, and use the product dimension formula [lem-sfb-abelian-finite-product]. Since $0<\dim B<\dim A$, both $\dim B$ and $\dim C$ are strictly smaller than $\dim A$. This establishes precisely the smaller dimensions needed below.

source.place: I Proposition 10.1, printed p.42, simple-factor discussion p.43, and Remark 8.6, p.36; scheme-theoretic details as specified in each step.

proof.text: Apply strong induction on $\dim A$ to obtain the simple-factor decomposition. For dimension zero, [lem-sfb-abelian-finite-product] identifies $A$ with the empty product. For positive dimension, if $A$ is $k$-simple take the one factor $A$ and the identity isogeny. Otherwise the definition in the statement supplies $B$ with $0<\dim B<\dim A$, and steps 1–3 give $s:B\times C\to A$ with both dimensions smaller. The induction hypothesis gives isogenies $u_B:\prod C_i\to B$ and $u_C:\prod D_j\to C$. Their product, followed by $s$, is the required homomorphism; it is an isogeny by the finite-map verification in the next step.

source.place: I Proposition 10.1, printed p.42, simple-factor discussion p.43, and Remark 8.6, p.36; scheme-theoretic details as specified in each step.

proof.text: Here is that verification for arbitrary isogenies. By [lem-sc-isogeny-degree] an isogeny is finite and flat. A product of two such maps factors as $u_B\times1$ followed by $1\times u_C$, each a base change of one factor; finiteness is preserved by base change and composition by [lem-trf-finite-radicial-basechange]. The maps are surjective: after passing to any algebraically closed extension of a target residue field, each nonempty finite fibre has a point, so the product fibre does too. Composition preserves surjectivity. The composite with $s$ is therefore finite and surjective; its kernel is finite by the base-change assertion of the same cited node, applied along the identity section. This proves that the composite is an isogeny [def-sc-isogeny] and completes the induction.

source.place: I Proposition 10.1, printed p.42, simple-factor discussion p.43, and Remark 8.6, p.36; scheme-theoretic details as specified in each step.

proof.text: Let $f:X\to Y$ be a nonzero homomorphism between $k$-simple abelian varieties. By [lem-sfb-abelian-hom-image-dimension] its image $I\hookrightarrow Y$ is an abelian subvariety. It has positive dimension: otherwise [lem-sfb-abelian-finite-product] makes it the zero abelian variety and $f=0$. Simplicity of $Y$ therefore forces $\dim I=\dim Y$. A closed subvariety of the integral finite-dimensional variety $Y$ of full dimension is all of $Y$: a chain in a proper irreducible closed subset extends strictly by $Y$, and any full-support closed subscheme has zero ideal in a reduced scheme. Integrality is supplied by [lem-sc-abelian-variety-characterization]. Thus $f$ is surjective.

source.place: I Proposition 10.1, printed p.42, simple-factor discussion p.43, and Remark 8.6, p.36; scheme-theoretic details as specified in each step.

proof.text: By [lem-sfb-abelian-kernel-abelian-part], $K=\ker f$ contains an abelian subvariety $D\subseteq X$ with $\dim D=\dim K$. By simplicity of $X$, $\dim D$ is zero or $\dim X$. In the second case the closed-subvariety argument of step 6, now using integrality of $X$ [lem-sc-abelian-variety-characterization], gives $D=X$ and hence $f=0$, a contradiction. Therefore $\dim K=0$, and the finite-kernel conclusion of the cited kernel lemma applies even if $K$ is nonreduced. Along with step 6 this proves that $f$ is an isogeny [def-sc-isogeny].

source.place: I Proposition 10.1, printed p.42, simple-factor discussion p.43, and Remark 8.6, p.36; scheme-theoretic details as specified in each step.

proof.text: Now let $f:X\to Y$ be any isogeny and $K=\ker f$. It is finite and flat by [lem-sc-isogeny-degree], and surjective by [def-sc-isogeny]; hence $\{f\}$ is an fpqc covering [def-weil-pbc-fpqc-covering]. Indeed the inverse image of an affine open is affine by finiteness and maps onto that open. The finite commutative group scheme $K$ is annihilated by its positive order $n$ by [lem-sfb-finite-group-scheme-order-annihilator]; commutativity follows from [lem-sc-av-commutative]. Thus $[n]_X$ vanishes on $K$ scheme-theoretically, not just on geometric points.

source.place: I Proposition 10.1, printed p.42, simple-factor discussion p.43, and Remark 8.6, p.36; scheme-theoretic details as specified in each step.

proof.text: The group laws [def-sc-group-scheme, def-sc-mult-n] identify $X\times_Y X$ with $X\times_kK$: $(x,t)\mapsto(x,x+t)$ has inverse $(x,x\prime)\mapsto(x,x\prime-x)$. Both are scheme morphisms assembled from the group operations; the inverse lands in $K$ because $f(x\prime-x)=0$. On this kernel pair the two pullbacks of $[n]_X$ are equal, since $[n](x+t)=[n]x+[n]t=[n]x$. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-fpqc-representable-descent] to obtain a unique scheme morphism $g:Y\to X$ with $gf=[n]_X$. It is over $k$: the two maps $Y\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ agree after precomposing with $f$, and uniqueness in the same descent lemma cancels $f$.

source.place: Tag 023Q, lemma-fpqc-universal-effective-epimorphisms; scheme-theoretic expansion of Milne AV I Remark 8.6, p.36.

proof.text: Check that $g$ is a homomorphism. Write $L=g m_Y$ and $R=m_X(g\times g)$ on $Y\times Y$. Pullback along $f\times f$ gives $L(fx,fx\prime)=[n](x+x\prime)$ and $R(fx,fx\prime)=[n]x+[n]x\prime$, equal by [def-sc-mult-n]. Each of $f\times1$ and $1\times f$ is an fpqc covering by [lem-galois-fpqc-covering-base-change]. Uniqueness in [lem-weil-pbc-fpqc-representable-descent] cancels these maps successively to give $L=R$. Also $g e_Y=gf e_X=[n]e_X=e_X$, and $(g i_Y)f=[n]i_X=i_X[n]=(i_Xg)f$, so the same uniqueness cancels $f$ and proves inverse compatibility. These are exactly the homomorphism identities [def-sc-group-scheme].

source.place: Tag 023Q, lemma-fpqc-universal-effective-epimorphisms; base change of coverings: Topologies Tag 022D, lemma-fpqc, part (3).

proof.text: Finally $(fg)f=f[n]_X=[n]_Yf$ by [def-sc-mult-n] and the homomorphism law. Uniqueness in [lem-weil-pbc-fpqc-representable-descent] cancels $f$, giving $fg=[n]_Y$. The equality $gf=[n]_X$ makes $g$ surjective because $[n]_X$ is surjective by [lem-sc-mult-n-isogeny]. The other equality embeds $\ker g$ as a closed subgroup scheme of $Y[n]$, which is finite by that same cited theorem. Its coordinate algebra is a quotient of a finite-dimensional $k$-algebra, so $\ker g$ is finite. Thus $g$ is an isogeny [def-sc-isogeny], and both required identities hold for the same $n>0$.
